issues.subcategory: Actual report delay contradicts short-delay claims
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly interprets the short conditions as probing memory within 0.5–0.75 s, but in the described procedures participants often did not report until after an irrelevant display presented several seconds later. Thus the measured response may reflect memory/decision processes occurring over ~4–6 s, not the claimed subsecond interval. This directly undermines the central claim that high-confidence illusions arise within 1–2 seconds or at 500 ms.
issues.quote: "If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset... In all cases, the memory probe was shown for 0.5 seconds and the irrelevant second display was presented for 0.5 seconds."

issues.subcategory: Cue timing misinterpreted as memory report timing
issues.description: The delay manipulation changes when a spatial cue/probe appears, not necessarily when the participant retrieves and reports the item. A cue can prioritize, consolidate, or protect an item in working memory, so differences between short and long cue conditions cannot be interpreted straightforwardly as passive memory decay or as the time course of illusion formation.
issues.quote: "In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display."

issues.subcategory: Increase over time does not prove memory transformation
issues.description: The authors infer that increased errors at longer delays must reflect ongoing transformation of correctly encoded memories. However, increases could arise from differential attention to the cue, decision noise, response bias at test, loss of orientation information, source confusion, or selective survival of high-confidence trials. The design does not isolate a mechanism that converts a correct representation into an illusory one.
issues.quote: "This effect must be due to processes ongoing in STM: Had these illusory memories been the result of changes in perception, they should have been present at the earlier probe as well."

issues.subcategory: No immediate perception/encoding control
issues.description: The study lacks a condition in which perception is tested while the display is present or immediately after offset without subsequent cueing, delay, interference, and recognition choices. Therefore the design cannot cleanly distinguish perceptual misencoding from early memory, response-selection, or test-induced effects.
issues.quote: "To rule out that these errors reflect a perceptual error that has directly been encoded into STM, we test whether illusory responses increase over time."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 critical trials often omitted the correct target
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display sometimes contained the mirrored counterpart instead of the actual target, making the correct response "none of these." Selecting the counterpart in such trials is not directly comparable to choosing between target and counterpart; it is confounded with use of the none option, forced-choice tendencies, and recognition-array design.
issues.quote: "If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials."

issues.subcategory: Unequal and unclear chance baselines for error types
issues.description: The analysis compares "illusory errors" with "other errors" as if they were equivalent outcomes, but the number and nature of available response alternatives differ. A mirrored counterpart is typically one option, whereas "other" errors may aggregate several distractors, memory items, or new items. Without modeling response-option base rates or chance probabilities, a main effect of Error Type is not a valid standalone test that illusions exceed an appropriate baseline.
issues.quote: "We investigated our three main hypotheses: hypothesis 1 - do illusions occur in STM? – by determining if participants confused pseudo-letter targets with their real counterpart with high confidence, or the other way around, more often than other high confidence errors (main effect of Error Type)."

issues.subcategory: High confidence is equated with false memory experience
issues.description: The manuscript defines memory illusions primarily as high-confidence errors. Confidence does not establish that participants had a phenomenological false memory rather than a fluent/familiar response, criterion bias, strategic inference, or metacognitive miscalibration. This threatens the construct validity of the central dependent variable.
issues.quote: "Therefore, isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there."

issues.subcategory: High-confidence threshold not defined
issues.description: The analyses repeatedly refer to "high confidence" trials, but the threshold used to classify confidence responses is not clearly specified, especially in Experiments 2–4 with a 1–4 scale. Replication and interpretation require knowing whether only the maximum rating, the top two ratings, or another rule was used.
issues.quote: "After this the participant first chose the target letter from 6 different response options, and then indicated her confidence (on a scale from 1 - 4)."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 confidence scale contradiction
issues.description: Experiment 1 is described inconsistently as using a 1–4 confidence scale in the figure caption but a two-point 1–2 confidence scale in the procedure. This affects the definition of "high confidence" and comparability across experiments.
issues.quote: "Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty)."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 participant numbers do not add up
issues.description: The manuscript states that 40 participants remained after training exclusions, but the analysis reports inclusion of 23 participants with only 5 excluded for too few high-confidence trials. These numbers are incompatible; 40 minus 5 is 35, not 23. The final analytic sample and attrition are therefore unclear.
issues.quote: "45 participants started training, 5 participants were excluded based on their training results. The remaining 40 participants..."

issues.subcategory: Large exclusions based on confidence responses
issues.description: A substantial fraction of participants was excluded after data collection because they had too few high-confidence trials. In Experiment 2, 92 of 290 participants were excluded. Since excluded participants had much lower high-confidence rates, the analyzed sample is a selected subgroup and may overestimate high-confidence illusions or alter condition effects.
issues.quote: "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded)."

issues.subcategory: Post hoc exclusion rule not preregistered
issues.description: The exclusion criterion based on having more than 10 high-confidence trials per cell is consequential and removes many participants, but the manuscript does not state that this rule was preregistered or justified a priori. This creates researcher degrees of freedom in defining the analyzed sample.
issues.quote: "Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion..."

issues.subcategory: Listwise deletion of missing cells
issues.description: Experiment 3 excludes a participant from the main ANOVA because of missing high-confidence responses in one or more cells. Missingness is directly related to confidence and possibly task performance, so listwise deletion may bias estimates unless sensitivity analyses or appropriate mixed models are provided.
issues.quote: "Because of listwise deletion of missing values (resulting from 0 high confidence responses in one or more of the cells of the design), one participant was excluded from the main ANOVA."

issues.subcategory: Confidence distributions by condition missing
issues.description: Because the core analyses condition on high-confidence trials, confidence rates by target type, delay, error type, and experiment are essential. The manuscript reports only overall high-confidence rates for included/excluded participants, preventing evaluation of whether condition effects are artifacts of conditioning on confidence.
issues.quote: "Included participants had on average 49.2% high confidence trial over all conditions (range: 24.6 – 95.8, sd: 13.3)."

issues.subcategory: ANOVA on aggregated bounded proportions
issues.description: The dependent variables are proportions derived from binomial trial counts with variable denominators after filtering to high-confidence trials. Repeated-measures ANOVA on aggregated proportions can violate distributional assumptions, ignore differing precision across cells, and mishandle missing cells. A trial-level binomial/multinomial mixed model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: "The relative occurrence of illusory memories (on high confidence trials) was analyzed in an ANOVA with target type (real or pseudo letter), interval (short or long) and type of error... as independent variables."

issues.subcategory: Participant-only aggregation ignores item/letter effects
issues.description: The analyses aggregate across letter identities and do not model random effects of specific letters or letter pairs. Some letters may be more visually confusable, more familiar, easier to verbalize, or asymmetrically biased when mirrored. Ignoring item variability limits generalization beyond the sampled letters and can inflate evidence for effects.
issues.quote: "For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors... was calculated."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 2 Table 4 contradicts reported result
issues.description: The text says that for non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was relevant and reports BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay. The displayed table instead shows Memory Delay BFincl = 0.064 and Target Type BFincl = 39110.895. This is a serious internal statistical inconsistency that changes the interpretation of the follow-up analysis.
issues.quote: "For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor... Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)"

issues.subcategory: Experiment 4 numerical comparison reversed
issues.description: The manuscript says the increase was smaller for mirrored targets than real-letter targets, but the reported percentages are 5% versus 4%, which is the opposite.
issues.quote: "There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference)."

issues.subcategory: Incorrect figure reference in Experiment 4
issues.description: The Experiment 4 results refer to Figure 5 even though the Experiment 4 figure is labeled Figure 6. This is minor but indicates reporting inconsistency.
issues.quote: "Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials."

issues.subcategory: General discussion misstates short probe timing
issues.description: The General Discussion states that Experiments 1 and 2 probed memory at 500 ms, but Experiment 1 used a 0.75 s cue and delayed report until after a later display; Experiment 2 also involved later report after the second display. The timing claim is therefore inaccurate.
issues.quote: "Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms (Experiment 1 and 2)"

issues.subcategory: Bayesian prior settings not reported
issues.description: Bayes factors are central to the analyses and to sequential stopping in Experiments 3–4, but the manuscript does not report the prior distributions, scale parameters, model priors, or robustness checks used in JASP. Bayes factors can be sensitive to these choices.
issues.quote: "The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4"

issues.subcategory: Overstated Bayes-factor interpretation threshold
issues.description: The manuscript labels BF < 0.33 as "strong evidence" for the null. Many conventional interpretive schemes treat values near 1/3 as only moderate/substantial evidence, with stronger evidence requiring smaller values. This risks overstating null evidence, especially for failed effects such as cue color.
issues.quote: "BF < 0.33: strong evidence for the null hypothesis. 0.33 - 1: substantial evidence for the null hypothesis."

issues.subcategory: Sequential Bayesian stopping insufficiently specified
issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used optional stopping based on a Bayes factor, but the manuscript does not fully specify the exact test, prior, planned sampling schedule, maximum sample size, or whether all analyses followed the stopping rule. Optional stopping with Bayes factors can be valid only under well-defined assumptions that are not reported here.
issues.quote: "Sample size was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test... Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 6, testing would stop."

issues.subcategory: Convenience sample without prospective power rationale
issues.description: Experiment 2's sample size was determined by course enrollment rather than a prospective design or precision target. Although large, this does not substitute for an a priori rationale for the key effects, exclusion-adjusted sample size, or planned stopping.
issues.quote: "The number of participants was determined not by the experimenter but by student enrollment in the course, which explains the large increase in participants compared to Experiment 1."

issues.subcategory: Online visual experiment lacks display and timing control
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online on participants' own laptops while stimuli are specified in visual angles and brief presentation durations. Without calibration of screen size, viewing distance, refresh rate, browser timing, or participant environment, stimulus size and exposure duration are uncontrolled and may not match laboratory experiments.
issues.quote: "the data was collected in an online experiment... each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop."

issues.subcategory: Stimulus rendering details incomplete
issues.description: The manuscript does not fully specify critical rendering details such as font, letter size in the main experiments, exact set of included letters, case, antialiasing, monitor characteristics, refresh rate, or viewing distance. These details are necessary to replicate a brief visual-memory task with mirrored letters.
issues.quote: "The memory and cue displays were set up in the same way as the displays in the training session, with 6 or 8 letters replacing the tilted bars."

issues.subcategory: Real versus pseudo letters confounded with familiarity and verbal codability
issues.description: Real letters and mirrored pseudo-letters differ not only in world-knowledge consistency but also in familiarity, nameability, verbal rehearsal, processing fluency, and possibly encoding precision. The design cannot isolate "world knowledge" from these correlated properties.
issues.quote: "Pseudo-letter were mirrored (i.e. flipped from left to right). Therefore only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment"

issues.subcategory: Orientation-feature loss alternative
issues.description: Participants may encode the letter identity correctly but lose or misremember the mirror-orientation feature. Reporting C after Ɔ could reflect loss of orientation information combined with default letter naming, not a rich false memory that the real letter was seen.
issues.quote: "participants were instructed to report the letter that appeared at the cued location. They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters"

issues.subcategory: World-knowledge causal claim not directly tested
issues.description: The conclusion that world knowledge drives the effect rests mainly on pseudo-to-real asymmetry. There is no direct manipulation of world knowledge, literacy, script familiarity, or long-term exposure, so alternative mechanisms such as response bias, verbal coding, or differential perceptual fluency remain viable.
issues.quote: "This suggests that world knowledge is a more important driver of illusory memories than visual similarity"

issues.subcategory: Response bias dismissal unsupported
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that participants may be biased to select real letters but dismiss this explanation without a formal signal-detection or multinomial response model. A real-letter response criterion or familiarity bias could produce high-confidence pseudo-to-real selections, especially in recognition arrays containing familiar real letters.
issues.quote: "Yet another reason why illusory reports arise could be a response bias: Participant might just be more inclined to select real letters instead of pseudo-letters... However, this is unlikely because the pattern of responses across conditions is consistent with memory-driven processes rather than response bias."

issues.subcategory: Recognition display may induce or bias reported illusion
issues.description: Because the response screen explicitly presents the real/pseudo counterpart, the test display itself may cue reconstruction, induce familiarity, or bias selection. The study lacks an open-report or neutral probe condition to show that the illusory content existed before the response alternatives were shown.
issues.quote: "The response screen consisted of 6 letters, 3 real letters and their pseudo counterparts... Since the target letter (and its counterpart) were always among the response options"

issues.subcategory: Irrelevant second display may create source confusion
issues.description: A second letter display appears before response and is only described as randomly selected and unrelated. The manuscript does not report constraints ensuring that it could not contain the target, counterpart, or visually similar items, nor analyses of whether second-display content affected errors. This creates a source-monitoring confound.
issues.quote: "To increase memory decay through task-irrelevant interference, a second display was included in each trial. This display consisted of randomly selected letters, unrelated to the memory display. Participants were instructed to ignore this second display."

issues.subcategory: Interference condition confounds memory interference with cue perception
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the cue appears together with the irrelevant second display in the Short-with-interference condition. This may impair cue localization or attention at retrieval, not just increase memory decay through visual interference.
issues.quote: "If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition)."

issues.subcategory: Cue-color expectation manipulation weak and confounded
issues.description: The red and blue cues differed in luminance and target probabilities, but the study provides no behavioral evidence that participants learned or used the contingency. The null effect therefore does not support the conceptual conclusion that transient expectations require substantial time to influence memory.
issues.quote: "both the central fixation cross and the cue were either blue (CIE: 0.148, 0.078, luminance: 6.47 cd/m2) or red (CIE: 0.641, 0.341; luminance: 11.9 cd/m2)."

issues.subcategory: Overinterpretation of null cue-color effect
issues.description: The authors infer from a null effect that expectations need substantial time to develop. But the manipulation may have been unnoticed, weak, underlearned, or confounded by color/luminance; absence of evidence for this manipulation is not evidence for a general theory of expectation formation.
issues.quote: "However, transiently generated expectations... had no effect on the prevalence of illusory memories. This is consistent with the notion that expectations need substantial time to develop before they can affect explicit, high confidence memories."

issues.subcategory: Feedback may alter priors and strategies
issues.description: Participants received repeated trial-level or block-level feedback, which could train them about base rates of real versus pseudo targets and encourage response strategies. The manuscript does not analyze learning over time or separate effects of lifelong priors from experiment-induced contingencies.
issues.quote: "After each trial the participant received feedback (correct/ incorrect response) on her performance. The main experiment consisted of 12 blocks of 20 trials. After each block the participant received feedback on her performance which included information about her average accuracy."

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 training selection limits comparability
issues.description: Experiment 1 excluded participants using a separate visual-memory training task with rectangles. This selects for motivated/high-performing visual-memory participants and was not applied consistently across experiments, limiting comparability and generalizability.
issues.quote: "Participants could only participate in the actual experiment, if they scored higher than 75% correct (averaged across all trials) on the final 10 blocks of training."

issues.subcategory: Narrow student Latin-letter sample
issues.description: The sample consists largely of young psychology students familiar with the Latin alphabet. Claims about short-term memory generally, or about world knowledge broadly reshaping memory, may not generalize to other ages, cultures, scripts, literacy levels, or non-letter stimuli.
issues.quote: "The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum."

issues.subcategory: Broad conclusion exceeds stimulus domain
issues.description: The experiments use mirrored Latin letters, yet the conclusions are phrased broadly as properties of short-term memory and recent recollection in general. The manuscript should more clearly limit conclusions to familiar symbolic stimuli unless supported by other stimulus domains.
issues.quote: "In conclusion, four experiments consistently show that illusory memories arise even when the visual stimulus has only been out of sight for very brief periods of time."

issues.subcategory: Contradictory claim that all STM stages are susceptible
issues.description: The manuscript states that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories, but also acknowledges that iconic memory was not tested. This is an overclaim and an internal theoretical inconsistency.
issues.quote: "The fact that all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories has important implications for vision research"

issues.subcategory: WM/FM classification not operationally established
issues.description: The discussion labels conditions as working-memory or fragile-memory setups based on cue/interference structure, but the experiments do not independently measure capacity, durability, interference sensitivity, or other defining properties of these memory stores. The mapping from task condition to memory system is therefore speculative.
issues.quote: "Experiment 1 shows that when the memory cue is presented together with unrelated information, a trial-type most like a WM manipulation, illusory memories are highly prevalent. Experiment 2-4 show that in a FM set-up illusory memories are also abundant."

issues.subcategory: Faulty argument against fuzzy trace theory
issues.description: The manuscript argues that FTT predicts high similarity should facilitate false memories and then says the data are inconsistent because highly similar mirrored counterparts produced abundant false memories. That observation appears consistent with, not contrary to, the stated prediction.
issues.quote: "However, FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should facilitate false memories . This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant."

issues.subcategory: Misuse of FTT terminology
issues.description: The discussion appears to conflate FTT's "verbatim" trace with "verbal" representations and then builds an articulatory-rehearsal argument on that terminology. This conceptual slippage weakens the theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: "FTT does suggest that pseudo-letters have a verbal (the letter itself) and a gist level (“mirrored”) representation, while real letters can be stored purely at the verbal level."

issues.subcategory: Uncertainty intervals and effect-size precision absent
issues.description: The manuscript reports percentages and Bayes factors but generally omits confidence/credible intervals or standard errors for key condition means and contrasts. This limits assessment of effect magnitude, precision, and practical importance, especially with variable cell counts after high-confidence filtering.
issues.quote: "With pseudo-letter targets, a longer memory delay (from Short to Long) generated an 8% increase of expectation-induced memory illusions (from 25% to 33%)."

issues.subcategory: Awareness/manipulation check for color contingency inadequate
issues.description: The conclusion that the cue-color contingency was unnoticed is based on an open-ended questionnaire after the experiment. This is a weak manipulation check; it does not measure implicit learning, trial-wise expectancy, or whether participants noticed but failed to mention the contingency.
issues.quote: "Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses."
